articles.title: Who cares? Caregivers’ perspectives of non/encounters with autism in Singapore
articles.abstract: In the densely-populated city-state of Singapore, encounters between people with and without disability happen in close proximity and high frequency, setting the scene for deeper exploration of the role of non/encounters in shaping urban care. To do so, this paper draws on a thematic analysis of interviews and ‘go-along’ ethnographic observations with 18 caregivers of persons with autism, spotlighting three caregivers’ narratives. Using the term ‘non/encounters’ to emphasise the importance of both encounters and non-encounters as well as their relational nature in shaping experiences of urban care, this article demonstrates ways in which co-users of urban spaces can play a role in sharing care responsibilities alongside familial caregivers. In uncovering the intangible structures of social norms and past memories that shape non/encounters beyond their immediate moment of occurrence, this article informs how urban care can be experienced and achieved. Firstly, I illustrate the role of research in constituting and facilitating caring encounters. Next, I detail caregivers’ experiences of exclusionary encounters within ableist spaces, while exploring the possibilities of care within repeated encounters. Influenced by past negative encounters, I elucidate caregivers’ desire for non-encounters to minimise experiences of exclusionary encounters. Drawing from urban studies, disability and care research, this article emphasises the importance of a disability perspective in conceptualisations of urban care. Consequently, this paper contributes to urban care literature by demonstrating the conceptual relevance of non/encounters in a non-Western context, positioning care as a shared responsibility of the urban citizenry.

articles.title: Reclaiming space: Mushaʿ land and indigenous urbanization in Ain Al-Basha
articles.abstract: Historically, mushaʿ, or communal land, represented a system of collective land ownership and crop rotation that provided social and spatial control over land in Jordan. This system persisted until the British Mandate in the early 20th century, which redefined land ownership toward private control as a means of taxation and sovereignty over the colonized population. Drawing on archival research, mapping, and interviews, this article explores how members of a tribal group have reclaimed land by establishing parallel infrastructures on mushaʿ land along Jordan Street in Ain Al-Basha. This case advances two theoretical contributions to Indigenous urban studies and urban planning scholarship. First, it develops the concept of state flexibility, theorizing uneven and reactive state governance not as planning failure but as a deliberate, situational strategy through which regulations are selectively extended or suspended in relation to historically embedded constituencies. Second, it proposes the dialectic of intention and response as a framework for understanding how Indigenous urban space is co-produced through ongoing negotiation between community agency and state calculation, rather than through straightforward opposition or resistance. Together, these concepts expand the analytical scope of Indigenous urban studies beyond settler-colonial frameworks, foregrounding a global South context in which tribal or Indigenous groups are neither external to the state nor uniformly dispossessed, but deeply entangled in its political and institutional foundations.

articles.title: Gender homophily and rent premiums in platform-mediated shared housing: Evidence from Ziroom in urban China
articles.abstract: Digital platforms are increasingly reshaping how housing is accessed, priced, and experienced in cities. Platform logics, characterized by data-driven processes and algorithmic pricing, can reflect and reinforce existing social inequalities. This study examines how gender intersects with platform dynamics to shape rental outcomes in Nanjing, China, a major metropolis of nearly 10 million residents. Drawing on a year of data from 373,964 bedroom listings on Ziroom, the country’s largest shared rental platform, the study tests whether the gender composition of roommates influences rents. Hedonic regressions controlling for unit, building, and neighborhood characteristics show that all-female-roommate units command a rent premium, suggesting gender homophily is priced as a valued amenity. When interaction terms with room status are included, results show no initial rent difference under “reserve,” but a clear premium for all-female units under two leasing conditions: immediate move-in (“sign”) and subleasing (“sublease”). These findings suggest that the premium does not arise from platform-set base rents but from gendered preferences interacting with algorithmic pricing, whereby units with stronger demand are discounted less. This study contributes to research on platform-mediated housing, PropTech, and housing inequality by quantifying how platform systems reflect and reproduce gendered disadvantage. It also highlights the value of platform data for understanding emerging rental markets and calls for greater attention to gender in the governance of shared and platform-mediated housing.

articles.title: From data silos to data agency: The role of local sports communities as data agents in urban governance
articles.abstract: This study investigates the overlooked yet pivotal role of local sports communities (LSCs) as data agents in the collaborative governance of urban public spaces. Rather than framing citizens’ leisure sports solely as intervention, we develop a triadic framework, comprising Governance Structure, Data Production, and Decision Mediation, to analyze how LSCs generate, manage, and translate data for urban governance. Three integration patterns are identified through the theory-informed case studies ( n = 12). The findings show that LSCs function with multifaceted roles, providing trust and legitimacy, generating grounded data, and mobilizing narratives to shape governance pathways. Ultimately, we conclude with a Quadrant Model to map LSCs’ embeddedness along the axes of institutional legitimacy and grassroots agency, offering a diagnostic tool for tracing the evolution from data silos to active data agency. The study contributes to debates on data-driven urbanism, collaborative governance, and leisure sports.

articles.title: Corrigendum to Under the paving stones at the Bloordale Beach: Sub-terra urbs nullius and volumetric colonialism in Toronto
Measurements and distinctions, from urban to rural
Kashan’s path from ancient culture to the modern creative city
Integrating construction and solar expansion can reduce disposal and dependency
Hausberg urbanization in the European Alps

A global structural typology of cities from urban centers
Your place or mine? Overcoming neoliberal placemaking as commodification of built environments in the inclusive city
articles.abstract: This paper critiques the evolving role of placemaking within the neoliberal city, examining its implications for urban development and social equity. While placemaking ostensibly fosters community engagement and sustainable urban environments, it can beco-opted to commodify the built environment, exacerbating issues such as gentrification, displacement, and the erosion of local identity. Drawing on insights from an Urban Leisure and Tourism (ULT) Living Lab in Rotterdam, this research highlights how top-down regeneration efforts have marginalised vulnerable communities in the city under the guise of inclusive development. As concerns grow over the temporality of placemaking initiatives, this study calls for a critical reflection on placemaking as a social practice. The research explores how bottom-up, community-centred placemaking strategies can counter these trends by fostering resilience and socio-ecological equity. Focusing on economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods that are acutely affected by spatial change, the study investigates how communities can safeguard themselves from the extractive impacts of tourism and development while amplifying the voices of historically excluded stakeholders. Sharing insights and citizen perspectives from urban activation projects at the living lab, we advocate for systemic, participatory approaches to urban transformation that prioritize local ownership, inclusivity, and sustainable resource management. It challenges current practices that favour short-term economic gain over long-term societal well-being and seeks out transparent, community-driven models of urban planning that, that are taken seriously and acted upon by developers and policymakers rather than merely providing tokenistic acknowledgement. Such approaches are essential for creating more inclusive cities that genuinely reflect and serve the needs of all their residents.

articles.title: When transit stops: Causal evidence on travel times from a transit strike in Quebec city
Revealing urban vitality structures in South Korea: A nationwide analysis of 225 cities
Governance of overwork among migrant workers: Effective measures or effective beauty?
Culture as repair in Black Los Angeles? Destination Crenshaw and the possibilities of reparative development
articles.abstract: For decades, culture-based urban development strategies have proliferated in Black communities, yet scholarship has documented how such approaches, whether heritage-based development or creative economy initiatives, often reproduce displacement despite intentions to the contrary. Less examined is what happens when Black communities control the development process itself, and whether institutional control can fundamentally alter displacement dynamics. Drawing on two years of ethnographic research with Destination Crenshaw, a $100-million cultural development project in South Los Angeles, I develop reparative development as an analytical framework for understanding community-led cultural strategies that explicitly orient toward repair, redress, and futurity. The framework identifies five distinguishing dimensions: acknowledgment of historical harm, symbolic and material restitution, institutional restructuring, community self-determination, and future orientation. The findings reveal that reparative development achieves genuine gains (cultural permanence, economic pathways, institutional capacity) yet faces structural limitations that community control cannot transcend: the amenity trap, whereby cultural investment accelerates displacement; the temporal mismatch between slow repair work and fast-moving real estate markets; and the restitution gap between symbolic recognition and material redistribution. These findings suggest that cultural strategy represents one component of a broader repair agenda but cannot substitute for the structural transformations full repair demands.

articles.title: Urban–rural economic inequality in western China's reform frontier: Nighttime light-based insights from Chengdu–Chongqing
Government relocation and urban spatial reconstruction in China: Effects, mechanisms, and governance implications
Exploring the role of politicians and bureaucrats in governance of metropolitan areas. Experiences from Czechia
articles.abstract: Problems of governance are a recurring theme in research on metropolitan areas, yet the role of politicians, bureaucrats, and political-administrative relations remains underexplored. This article addresses this gap by analyzing political-administrative relations in the governance of Czech metropolitan areas. As metropolitan areas in Czechia were established relatively recently, it is possible to observe the dynamics between politicians and civil servants from their inception. Based on semi-structured interviews with politicians and civil servants from two metropolitan areas, the findings suggest that civil servants hold a relatively strong position due not only to their expertise and knowledge of EU funding opportunities and project management, but also to the limited interest of politicians in the metropolitan agenda. Politicians' low engagement appears to result from a focus on immediate economic benefits and difficulties navigating issues beyond electoral district boundaries. This passive political role contributes to the uncertain status of metropolitan areas, which lack strong political advocacy.

articles.title: Context-sensitive Sponge City strategies: A cross-case and multi-scalar analysis
articles.abstract: Sponge Cities are more than technical solutions to urban flooding–they are dynamic spaces where water, land, and society converge in adaptation and resilience. This study bridges theory and practice through a comparative, cross-case framework that analyzes Sponge City strategies across five Dutch lowland landscape types (coastal, riverine, peat, sandy, clay) and selected international contexts. Emphasizing scale as a critical dimension, the study explores how blue, green, and blue-green strategies are shaped by ecological conditions and local practices. Beyond hydrological performance, it highlights the often-overlooked social dimension, including community participation, equity, and social resilience. The research adopts a qualitative, interpretivist methodology, combining within-case and cross-case analysis. It unfolds in two phases: first, a global typology of 38 Sponge City strategies is developed, categorized as green, blue, or green-blue, and analyzed by spatial scale (site, neighborhood, city), sponge basin principles (protect, delay, store, release), and hydrological processes (infiltration, retention, storage, purification, utilization, drainage). The second phase offers an in-depth evaluation of eight Dutch projects across Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Almere, Purmerend, and The Hague, examining ecological, spatial, and social performance through thematic coding and structured comparison. The findings highlight a gap between the coherence of Sponge City theory and its real-world application, particularly regarding social integration. Successful implementation depends on context-sensitive strategies that go beyond water management to include accessibility, inclusivity, and community engagement. This study contributes to a broader understanding of how human-centered, adaptive design can support climate resilience across diverse urban landscapes, grounding its analysis in a landscape-based Sponge City framework that links Sponge Basin principles (protect, delay, store, release) with lowland landscape typologies and cross-scalar design strategies.

articles.title: Classification of medium and small cities for the implementation of Low Emission Zones
articles.abstract: Growing mobility within cities has led to an unacceptable increase in the negative externalities of transport. In order to reduce this negative impact, Low Emission Zones (LEZs) are being implemented; among other actions and objectives, they include some type of circulating restriction for vehicles to improve air quality. Given the differences among cities, and the great variety of measures that a LEZ may include, it is necessary to develop aids for choosing the most appropriate type of LEZ to be implemented. This study identifies groups of cities having similar geophysical and socioeconomic characteristics, as well as other traits related with the generation of negative impacts by transport. Our classification may be used to propose common policy guidelines —in some cases even specific proposals— for planning an adequate LEZ in each city group, or for other municipalities that could identify with a particular group.The study case is Spain. A total of 61 cities were considered, described by means of 11 variables. Cluster analysis was used to define the groups of cities, giving eight clusters; in view of their most relevant characteristics, different policy guidelines and actions could be put forth for the design of a particular LEZ for each group.

articles.title: Assessing the economic effects of micromobility sharing using credit card transaction data: Evidence from accessibility, mobility, and connectivity
Manufacturing the urban: Situating manufactured housing and manufactured home communities in urban studies and charting a course for research
articles.abstract: Manufactured housing (MH) provides a key source of affordable housing in the United States and elsewhere, including in Canada and Australia. In this editors’ introduction, we argue that MH and manufactured home communities (MHCs) deserve more attention from researchers, planners, and policy makers because they are home to millions of people and because they provide a lens through which to understand critical contemporary issues in the study of housing and urban settlements more broadly. We provide an overview, define key terms, and describe the scale, and some advantages and disadvantages of manufactured housing. The introduction also defines manufactured home communities (also commonly called by other names, including “mobile home parks” and “trailer parks”) and describes their broad diversity. We introduce the articles in the special issue, summarizing key areas of concern that shape housing affordability, security, and equity for residents of MH and MHCs. These include: (1) regulation and location of manufactured housing; (2) housing tenure, ownership, and finance; (3) resident experience, social relations, and politics in manufactured home communities; and (4) hazards and climate change. This introduction and the other articles in this issue make the case that manufactured housing should be repositioned from the margins to the center of scholarship on housing and urbanism because the challenges facing manufactured housing residents, from financialization and tenure insecurity to heightened climate change vulnerability, are relevant and revelatory for research in other marginalized communities and housing types around the world.

articles.title: Housing insecurity and conflict in Nairobi: Comparing the dynamics of low-income urban settlements
articles.abstract: Rapid urbanization often fuels the expansion of low-income settlements, where competition over space and scarce economic opportunities can spark violent conflict. Such settlements are characterized by insufficient infrastructure, low-quality housing, and are often built informally on public land; yet in reality, the extent and dynamics of housing insecurity vary extensively, as does the extent to which housing insecurity becomes a focal point of political and intergroup conflict. We argue that the way in which these settlements were established and grew over time, along with local political dynamics, and macro-level government policies condition how housing insecurity intersects with urban conflict. We study these dynamics through a comparative analysis of two settlements in Nairobi: Korogocho and Kawangware. Drawing on rich empirical data—a survey, interviews and focus groups—our analysis advances understanding of how housing insecurity intersects with political and intergroup conflict and contributes to key debates about the impact of informality and formality on urban insecurity and conflict, as well as to the literature on historical claims to land as a central driver of urban conflict. In essence, diverse historical origins of low-income settlements shape local political dynamics and claim-making in ways that create distinct pathways to housing insecurity and its potential to generate collective mobilization.

articles.title: Building age diversity and retail patterns: A morphometric exploration of Jacobs’ neglected condition through the Temporal Fingerprint Matrix
articles.abstract: Jane Jacobs established diversity as the cornerstone of urban vitality, arguing that four conditions – mixed primary uses, small blocks, buildings varying in age and concentration of people – generate the exuberant diversity essential for vibrant cities. Recognizing retail patterns as indicators of urban vitality, urban studies has extensively tested three conditions, while building age diversity remains the least examined. The few existing studies have produced conflicting findings due to limitations in how building age characteristics are measured. To address these gaps, we introduce the Temporal Fingerprint Matrix, a novel analytical framework integrating building age and age diversity to distinguish incremental from instant development patterns. Aligned with Jacobs’ theoretical framework, we hypothesize that incrementally developed areas, characterized by diverse building ages and substantial older building stock, demonstrate higher retail density and diversity compared to instantly developed areas with uniform and predominantly newer buildings. Analysing approximately 600,000 buildings across Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Den Haag, we employ hierarchical clustering and identify distinct development types. Statistical analysis examines whether these types systematically influence retail density and diversity. Results reveal seven distinct development types with significantly different retail patterns and confirm our hypothesis: incrementally developed areas consistently outperform instantly developed areas in retail density and diversity. This study fills a critical knowledge gap by providing the first systematic test of Jacobs’ most neglected diversity condition and introduces a replicable morphometric method for identifying temporal development patterns. The findings inform time-conscious planning strategies for enhancing retail density and diversity through balanced preservation-development approaches that cultivate age-diverse built environments.

articles.title: Assembling Community Wealth Building policies in Scotland: Policy mobilities, institutional translations and localised adaptations
articles.abstract: Against the backdrop of growing interest in Community Wealth Building (CWB) globally as a means of fostering local economic resilience and social equity, Scotland has emerged as a prominent site for experimentation and policy development in this domain. Drawing on qualitative analysis of semi-structured interviews conducted in three of the Scottish CWB pilot areas, and informed by literature on policy transfer, policy mobilisation, and new municipalism, this paper explores the assemblage of CWB policy in Scotland. By unpacking the dynamics of policy adaptation across local contexts with very different characteristics, this paper seeks to contribute to existing scholarship by advancing our understanding of new municipalism as a relational and plural field and it emphasises the importance of context-specific approaches in realising the transformative potential of CWB in Scotland and beyond.

articles.title: A caring smart city: A bottom-up approach with older adults in Santiago de Chile
articles.abstract: Age-friendly and smart-city agendas have developed in parallel: the former foregrounds older adults’ wellbeing but lacks operationalisation, with indicators under-capturing digital inclusion and pedestrian safety; the latter deploys data platforms treating older people as passive subjects within privately governed systems. Although care is increasingly recognised as a principle of urban governance, few studies examine how co-designing civic technologies with older adults can generate context-sensitive spatial metrics for municipal decision-making. This article asks: how can digital technologies be repurposed as infrastructures of care to strengthen older people’s right to the city in Global South contexts? Drawing on the Ciudad Mayor project (2022–2024) in three municipalities of Santiago de Chile, a sequential mixed-methods design is employed: participatory collective mapping with older residents; iterative co-design and usability testing of a mobile app; and geospatial analysis producing ‘‘‘hyper-cartographies’’’ — maps combining citizen-generated reports with objective indicators. Participatory mapping revealed micro-barriers — such as uneven pavements and poor lighting — that escape standardised indicators but condition everyday mobility. The co-designed app functioned as a traceable channel linking older people’s situated knowledge to neighbourhood budgeting. Older participants demonstrated strong capacity to engage with accessible digital tools. Conceptually, infrastructures of care are positioned as a bridge between age-friendly and smart-city debates. Methodologically, a replicable protocol integrating co-design with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) is proposed to produce context-sensitive metrics, reframing the smart city as a democratic, age-affirming project rather than a techno-managerial fix.

articles.title: Urban climate vulnerability, housing and drug supply
The Indian street dog crisis and multispecies coexistence in tropical urban futures
Urban green credits: Capturing ecosystem service value in housing markets for redistributive urban planning
articles.abstract: Urban green infrastructure generates substantial ecosystem services, yet the economic value of these benefits is often captured privately through housing markets rather than reinvested in public ecological provision. This paper addresses this gap by introducing Urban Green Credits (UGC), a planning-oriented framework that links ecological performance to fiscal instruments. We develop a parcel-level Index of Ecosystem Services (IES) integrating carbon sequestration, thermal regulation, ecological connectivity, and accessibility to green spaces. Using 5230 residential transactions in Porto, Portugal, we estimate the capitalisation of ecological performance into housing prices through hedonic, spatial econometric, instrumental variable, and difference-in-differences models. Results show that ecosystem services are consistently and significantly reflected in property values, with robust effects across specifications and identification strategies. Building on these estimates, we simulate the fiscal potential of UGC, demonstrating that even modest capture rates can generate meaningful revenues and support redistribution towards ecologically underserved areas. The findings contribute to bridging ecosystem service valuation and urban fiscal policy, advancing a framework that integrates environmental performance, land markets, and equity considerations. While conceptual and requiring contextual calibration, UGC provides a novel pathway for financing urban greening while addressing spatial inequalities.

articles.title: Imagining economic development, enabling sprawl: Planning for logistics in suburban regions
Environment-adjusted port efficiency and port-industry-city coupling coordination: Lessons from China's coastal port clusters
“Tire Operation” model: A disaster-driven hybrid framework for assessing ecological resilience and guiding spatial planning in hazard-prone communities
The restorative power of blue spaces: A 19-country study
articles.abstract: Living in urbanised areas can deplete cognitive and emotional resources. To help restore them, many people seek out natural locations. Blue spaces (e.g. rivers, lakes, coasts) are among people’s favourite restorative settings, but we know little about the importance of type or quality for psychological restoration, or the role of nature connectedness. Using survey data from 19 countries (n = 17,131), we explored the extent to which participants perceived a recent blue space visit had helped them “rest and recover [their] abilities to focus” and feel “part of nature”. Seventeen blue space types were investigated, spanning marine, lentic (‘standing’) inland, and lotic (‘flowing’) inland waters in both more natural and more built settings, respectively. Accounting for country differences, linear mixed models found all blue space settings were recalled as restorative, with sandy beaches and rural rivers/canals the most, and marshlands the least. Recalled nature connectedness was also high overall, although more natural blue spaces consistently scored higher than built ones. Perceived safety was the quality indicator most associated with both outcomes. Actively engaging with the water (e.g. swimming, paddling) was associated with greater restoration than remaining on-land, and both outcomes showed diminishing marginal returns over time, peaking around 3 h. Path analysis focusing on walking (the most common visit activity) suggested a reciprocal relationship between perceived restoration and nature connectedness. Results provide multi-country evidence that spending recreational time at safe blue spaces can benefit diverse populations by helping them to restore depleted cognitive/emotional resources and connect with the natural world.

articles.title: Bird-mediated cultural ecosystem services and disservices depend on urban residents’ perceptions of birds
articles.abstract: Urbanization influences how people interact with nature, modifying perceptions of nature’s benefits (ecosystem services) or harms (ecosystem disservices or ED). In urban areas, wildlife-mediated ecosystem services remain understudied despite their importance for human well-being, particularly cultural ecosystem services (CES). The provision of species-mediated CES and ED also depends on the composition of wildlife communities, which can vary within cities. Urban areas can be developed in a gradient that goes from a scattered development (low-density housing with dispersed green spaces such as gardens) to a clumped development (high-density housing with large green spaces such as parks). Previous studies suggest that species composition, including CES and ED providers, may shift along this gradient. Yet, it remains unclear whether variation in these services and disservices is driven by differences in human perception (i.e., perception hypothesis) or by changes in ecological provision (i.e., species assembly hypothesis). We investigated both hypotheses using a multidisciplinary approach combining 637 in-person surveys and bird censuses across three Mediterranean cities. Our study identified four key CES (identity, educational, inspirational and bequest), disservices, and their main service-providing species. CES and ED varied across the gradient (i.e. higher bequest in clumped development while higher disservices in scattered development), mainly due to differences in residents’ perceptions rather than changes in the underlying ecological provision. Perceptions were also shaped by socio-demographic factors. This information can help create conservation plans to enhance the perception of benefits and promoting CES-providing species, while minimizing the harms associated with urban birds.

articles.title: Measuring the unmeasurable: An intelligent and interactive evaluation addressing aesthetic performance of urban texture via CLIP and LLMs
Enhancing urban climate resilience via polycentric spatial structure in the pursuit of SDG 13 (Climate Action)
Navigating the state-market nexus: Private planning practices in Vietnam
articles.abstract: Across Asia, large-scale land redevelopments have become a defining feature of market-driven urbanization. In Vietnam, as in other rapidly urbanizing contexts, these projects are not only privately financed and developed but also planned by private consultants. While such private-sector practices are increasingly widespread in Asia, they have received limited scholarly attention, particularly regarding how they shape planning processes and professional agency. This paper advances urban scholarship by examining the role of private planners as key intermediaries in state–market urbanization regimes. Our analysis focuses on Vietnam’s “new urban areas,” large-scale master planned residential and mixed-use developments typically built on converted peri urban land. We situate planning practices for these developments within a hybrid governance regime that layers market-oriented reforms onto a persistent state-directed planning system. Drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with local professionals and an analysis of institutional and economic conditions, we analyze how these actors navigate the competing demands of regulatory constraints, profitability imperatives, and their own professional aspirations. Findings show that planners deploy adaptive strategies by aligning goals to produce functionally complete environments with market logics and leveraging regulatory frameworks to temper development pressures. Yet these strategies are bounded by the same structures they mobilize, limiting their capacity to address broader equity concerns or challenge a profit-oriented urban model. By interrogating how professional agency is constituted in such hybrid governance settings, this study contributes to scholarship on planning privatization and urban neoliberalization beyond the Global North, offering new insights into how planners mediate, sustain, and subtly reshape market-driven urbanization.

articles.title: Bridging social capital and intersectional alliance: Towards an integrated framework for interpreting urban solidarity
articles.abstract: This article develops a theoretical framework for analyzing urban solidarity by bringing the concept of social capital into dialogue with the feminist notion of intersectional alliance. While social capital has long been used to examine relational resources embedded in networks, it has often been criticized for utilitarian and economic reductionism. Conversely, the concept of intersectional alliance foregrounds political commitment and solidarity across difference, but remains analytically under-specified. The article argues that integrating these two perspectives allows solidaristic cooperation among heterogeneous actors to be analyzed as a relational configuration that combines political orientation with relational mechanisms of cooperation. The paper reconstructs the genealogies and limits of both concepts and compares them across three analytical dimensions—motivations, purpose, and solidarity—before proposing an integrated framework that seeks to contribute to urban studies by offering a conceptual vocabulary for analyzing solidaristic relations in cities. The objective of the integration is twofold: first, to politicize social capital by mitigating its utilitarian tendencies and emphasizing the often-overlooked dimensions of power and conflict; second, to operationalize the concept of intersectional alliance, making it analytically useful for investigating the resources activated within social relationships. In doing so, the framework provides a theoretical lens for examining urban solidarity, where heterogeneous actors stabilize cooperation under conditions of spatial proximity and conflict.

articles.title: Building future cities with civil engineers
Editorial Board
Beyond scenic views: an integrative review of visual research on heritage landscapes—themes, methods, and typologies across scales
articles.abstract: Visual landscape research on heritage landscapes has expanded rapidly since 1995, yet its themes, study objects, and methods remain dispersed across disciplinary traditions. This review synthesizes 203 peer-reviewed studies published between 1995 and 2025 using a three-layered analytical framework that combines thematic coding, VOSviewer-based keyword co-occurrence analysis, and exploratory cross-dimensional Sankey mapping. Thematic coding shows that the field is concentrated around analysis/evaluation and management/conservation themes, with study objects dominated by formally recognized and spatially bounded heritage landscapes and methods centered on perception-based empirical approaches, GIS-based analysis, digital documentation, mixed methods, and multi-criteria evaluation. Keyword co-occurrence and cross-dimensional mapping further show that these distributions are organized through recurring but uneven theme–object–method associations. Three gaps are especially evident: perceptual and spatial evidence are often weakly coupled; less formalized, everyday, hybrid, and cross-scalar heritage landscapes remain underrepresented; and visual evidence is inconsistently translated into assessment, planning, and management contexts. Based on these findings, the review develops a review-derived organizing synthesis that relates research themes, heritage landscape types and scales, and methodological approaches. This synthesis clarifies the current structure of visual heritage landscape research, identifies underexplored intersections, and provides a basis for more transparent comparison and future empirical work.

articles.title: The equity impact of bike-sharing on developing X-minute cities: A case study of 36 cities in Zhejiang Province, China
Shaping socio-functional urban identity: When morphometrics meet social media data to reveal neighbourhood structure and cores
From dematerialization to well-being in digital cities: The Melting–Relief–Vitality model for Montreal, London and Tokyo, 1900–2050
Measuring lockdown travel rebound: Experimental insights from the Hong Kong COVID-19 omicron outbreak
articles.abstract: While localized lockdowns emerged as pivotal Non-pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) during the mid-to-late phases of the COVID-19 pandemic, the precise impacts on residential mobility remain understudied, including pre-and post-lockdown travel comparisons, ‘bounce-back’, and long and short-term adjustments. Policymakers were particularly concerned about unanticipated viral transmission from undiagnosed asymptomatic carriers. This study investigates Hong Kong’s Restriction-testing Declaration (RTD) policy, a short-term localized lockdown strategy mainly targeting public housing estates (PHEs) during the omicron outbreak. Employing a Propensity Score Matching and Difference-in-Differences (PSM-DID) framework, we analyzed anonymized mobile positioning data from 117,370 resident’s mobile devices during omicron outbreak, to quantify the lockdown-induced mobility response, defined as the distance to maximum reach position (DMRP).Our findings reveal that RTD events generated substantial increases in the daily average increase of 1.20 km of DMRP over the two-week study duration, and exhibits an inverted-U-shaped rebound pattern in differed epidemic phases. In the rising phase, RTD immediately increased PHE residents’ DMRP by 0.89 km on the implementation day, and this effect persisted for 11 days, with the maximum surge occurring on post-RTD Day 5. In the peak phase, no immediate impact occurred on the implementation day. However, an increase of 1.04 km occurred one day later, and this effect continued for 5 days, reaching its maximum surge on post-RTD Day 2. No significant DMRP increase was observed for the declining phase. This is the first empirical study to investigate how localized lockdowns impact residents’ travel rebound and provides key insights for policymakers to understand unintended mobility responses.

articles.title: Impact of depopulated area designation policy on the population and employment in Japanese small and medium-sized cities
Examining dual exposure to traffic congestion and in-vehicle crowding among senior and regular cardholders using smart card data
articles.abstract: In urban travel, traffic congestion often results in prolonged travel times, while in-vehicle crowding causes physical discomfort. Bus passengers uniquely face dual exposure to both congestion (from shared road networks) and crowding (from shared vehicle space), which compounds health risks and undermines sustainable transport goals. Despite this, few studies examine these concurrent exposures or the socio-demographic disparities in who bears this burden, particularly critical for vulnerable populations like senior groups who may face disproportionate impacts. Using Beijing bus smart card data, we measure congestion and crowding levels to identify adverse travel patterns and infer passengers' home locations. We then apply statistical and random forest models to examine how socio-demographic characteristics shape exposure to these adverse conditions across different urban areas. The study reveals the spatial-temporal dynamics of congestion and crowding, the daily rhythms of adverse travel flow across urban spaces, and the socio-demographic characteristic disparities that shape differential exposures among senior and regular cardholders. The findings indicate that congestion concentrates in urban centers and suburban hubs during peak hours, while crowding tends to persist throughout the day on suburban-urban corridors. Urban residents experience more congestion but less crowding than suburban and rural residents. Senior cardholders experience shorter durations but higher rates of adverse conditions than regular cardholders. By revealing dual exposure patterns across space, time, and demographics, this study identifies where and when interventions are needed to reduce congestion for urban commuters and crowding for suburban riders.

articles.title: County-level new-type urbanization policy and city economic resilience: Evidence from a quasi-natural experiment of 2302 counties in China
COVID-19 as a spatial shock: Uneven land market dynamics in metropolitan areas
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic reshaped the spatial dynamics of metropolitan land markets in the Czech Republic. Using a large dataset of land transactions and a Bayesian Vector Autoregression with exogenous variables (BVARX), we show that the pandemic reinforced suburbanization patterns, primarily driven by demand shocks, while broader macroeconomic factors played only a complementary role. These effects were not uniform across cities. Large metropolitan areas experienced strong and persistent suburbanization pressures, whereas mid-sized cities exhibited more muted responses, reflecting differences in regional integration and economic centrality. These shifts persisted beyond the pandemic period, indicating a lasting transformation in spatial land market dynamics. Overall, our findings highlight that city-specific structural characteristics critically shape the transmission of demand shocks and underscore the need for coordinated metropolitan planning to address pressures on land use, housing affordability, and infrastructure capacity.

articles.title: Assessing household's vulnerability to urban flood based on AHP and TOPSIS method: A case study of the flood-prone area in Pakistan
Aligning transit provision with urban morphology: A diagnostic assessment of Porto and Cagliari
articles.abstract: Transit accessibility in cities is shaped not only by service provision but also by the extent to which transit networks align with the structural hierarchy of streets. This paper develops a reproducible, data-efficient framework that integrates angular segment analysis from Space Syntax, proximity-based transit catchments, and population-weighted exposure measures to assess how well transit stops correspond to high-integration corridors. Two indicators operationalise this assessment: the Gap Index, which identifies the share of population exposed to high-integration corridors lacking nearby transit service, and the Equity Ratio, which compares exposure levels across demographic groups. The framework is applied to Porto and Cagliari, two Mediterranean port cities that share comparable urban morphologies but exhibit contrasting mobility outcomes. Findings reveal a strong divergence. Porto demonstrates complete proximity coverage of its structurally high-integration corridors, indicating a close alignment between transit routing and the spatial configuration of the street network. However, Cagliari displays a pronounced proximity deficit, with a substantial share of high-integration corridors lying outside 300 m transit stop catchments. These results suggest that differences in accessibility between the two cities arise not from population distribution or morphological potential but from strategic choices in transit routing. The study shows how morphology-aware indicators can help planners detect accessibility gaps that conventional supply-side assessments overlook and highlights the value of integrating spatial configuration analysis into routine diagnostic practices. The proposed framework offers a transferable basis for monitoring alignment between street structure and transit provision, supporting more responsive and equitable mobility strategies in port-city contexts.

articles.title: A joint synthetic housing–household inventory
A CityGML extension for 3D modeling of pedestrian mobility space
articles.abstract: This paper presents a conceptual model of pedestrian mobility spaces in 3D city models. While conceptual models can be specified in various ways, we use standard elements of CityGML and an Application Domain Extension (ADE): The Pedestrian ADE extends CityGML 3.0 to incorporate key parameters related to the physical, legal, and regulatory aspects of pedestrian mobility environments. For this, the extension introduces new feature classes for vertical passages such as stairs and elevators, and adds attributes to existing CityGML classes to represent pedestrian-specific characteristics. The conceptual model is also implemented for demonstration and validation: A real-world case study in Melbourne, Australia, demonstrates the practical application of the Pedestrian ADE to model complex urban environments. Through visualizations, we show how the model can be applied to represent spaces where different types of pedestrians can , cannot , may , or must not walk. This work provides a standardized approach for detailed 3D modeling of pedestrian mobility spaces, supporting various applications in urban planning, transportation, and accessibility analysis.

articles.title: Estimating a CPI-based regional price parity index for US cities
articles.abstract: Geographic price differences confound comparisons of economic performance across cities by conflating nominal urban advantages with real differences in well-being. Existing tools only partially address this problem: the Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes a Regional Price Parity (RPP) Index that represents relative price levels in US cities and states, but it is available only annually since 2008 and with a publication lag, limiting its usefulness for historical or high-frequency analysis. To address this measurement gap, we use the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for 29 US cities to construct a CPI-based RPP, enabling consistent comparisons of urban economic performance over time at constant and comparable prices. We exploit standard price-parity properties using publicly available CPI data to estimate CPI-based RPPs at a higher frequency and over longer historical horizons. This results in a CPI-based RPP for any period with published CPI data, as far back as 1913 in some cities to the most recent observations. By separating nominal urban advantages from cost-of-living differences, the index allows researchers to reassess claims about urban well-being, affordability, and the real returns to agglomeration. We demonstrate the index by examining long-run regional price dynamics and comparing real per capita GDP and real per capita personal income across cities at constant and comparable prices.

articles.title: Should I stay or should I go: How urban heat gradients affect the local distribution of birds and bats
articles.abstract: Facing escalating biodiversity decline, threats extend beyond species loss to reduced evolutionary and functional potential in ecosystems. Urbanisation is one of the main causes of biodiversity loss, and its impact is expected to be further increased by the anticipated growth in the human population over the coming decades. In this context, achieving sustainable development requires a balance between conservation and urban growth. A key step in characterizing the impacts of urbanisation on biodiversity using integrative approaches that reflect current scenarios of global change. This study focuses on the main representatives of urban flying vertebrates, birds and bats, to study how different levels of urbanisation affect these components of biodiversity. More precisely, we examine the influence of Urban Heat Islands (UHIs), as a proxy of strong urbanisation, on community composition and taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional diversity of bats and birds in the French city of Poitiers. We also assess the contribution of turnover and nestedness to community composition. Our results indicate that high urbanisation, reflected by UHIs, affects community composition, particularly for bats, whose diversity across taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional components is reduced. In contrast, birds display only a decline in taxonomic diversity in these zones. Turnover is the dominant process structuring bird communities, whereas nestedness primarily drives bat assemblages, suggesting greater potential for species replacement in birds. These results highlight the differing vulnerability of birds and bats to urbanisation and emphasize the need to consider these differences and the ecological interactions between them in conservation and urban planning strategies.

articles.title: Blackbird movements and habitat selection inform restoration of functional connectivity across cities
articles.abstract: Although ecological restoration strategies are increasingly promoted to enhance biodiversity, ecosystem services and climate resilience in cities, little is known about their impact on functional connectivity. We integrated empirical movement data with spatially explicit connectivity modelling to assess how alternative urban restoration strategies may affect breeding habitat availability and functional connectivity for the common blackbird ( Turdus merula ) in Gijón (NW Spain). Telemetry data from 13 adults were used to assess home range size, movement distances and habitat selection within the urban matrix. This dataset allowed to parameterise resistance surfaces and identify potential breeding habitat patches, which served as nodes in a circuit-theory-based connectivity framework. To evaluate how different urban restoration strategies may influence habitat availability and connectivity, we compared three scenarios representing increasing levels of restoration intensity. Under baseline conditions, suitable breeding habitat was highly fragmented. Although nearly 10% of the study area was suitable, only one third was functionally connected. The “Connectors Restoration” scenario, adding small-scale linear connectors along streets, was predicted to substantially improve connectivity among existing patches despite it did not increase habitat availability. The “Targeted Restoration” scenario, promoting strategically selected public green areas, was associated with the highest efficiency, achieving large gains in habitat availability and connectivity with relatively limited restoration effort. The “Full Restoration” of all public green infrastructure yielded the largest absolute gains, but showed lower efficiency, indicating diminishing marginal returns at broader spatial scales. Overall, our results suggest that connectivity-informed planning may enhance landscape functioning in dense urban environments and highlight the importance of targeted restoration actions to maximise ecological outcomes under limited resources.

articles.title: Urban planning, the built environment, and subjective well-being: A review of recent research advances
articles.abstract: Research on how the built environment shapes subjective well-being has expanded rapidly since 2021, providing new insights for urban planning and policy. Yet, no review has synthesized major recent advances in this field. This narrative review synthesizes five categories of advances – (1) disruptions to urban life, (2) mobility and accessibility, (3) social and experiential dimensions, (4) planning paradigms and urban form, and (5) urban artificial intelligence (AI) – based on a pathways framework linking the built environment to subjective well-being. Recent evidence highlights the importance of walkability, proximity, green space, and housing quality in supporting well-being, particularly under conditions of constrained mobility or when time spent at home increases. A composite of meeting places can foster social interaction and urban vitality, promote inclusion, and help combat loneliness. Public transport investments, including new metro systems and high-speed rail, are associated with social interaction, prevention of exclusion, and subjective well-being. Access to a private car may enhance activity participation and opportunities, particularly in car-oriented environments, while producing important equity and sustainability externalities. Architecture and public space design influence emotional well-being, with traditional styles linked to positive emotional responses. The 15-minute city, urban vitality, high-rise living, telework, and urban AI represent urban concepts and digital developments that transform urban planning and subjective well-being. The outcomes of the review strengthen and enrich the pathways between built environment and subjective well-being and raise attention to inequalities between population groups and contexts.

articles.title: The implications of a land value tax on urban agglomeration dynamics: Efficiency and equity
articles.abstract: Cities have become widely recognised as pivotal hubs for economic growth, with continued evidence of productivity gains from density and proximity of agglomerations. However, the same externalities of dense urban agglomerations exert pressures on the built environments and are partially responsible for a deepening urban crisis (e.g., increasing wealth disparities, housing crisis), harming both equity and efficiency. While Land Value Taxation (LVT) is widely recognised for its potential to improve land use efficiency and affordability, its implications for agglomeration mechanisms remain overlooked. This article synthesises two largely disconnected bodies of literature—agglomeration theory and LVT—to open a debate on how taxing the unimproved value of land could realign incentives within rigid and exclusionary urban environments. Drawing on a systematic literature review and expert interviews, we identify a notable conceptual gap but strong theoretical compatibility. We argue that LVT can enhance the spatial, temporal, and interactive domains of agglomeration by internalising externalities where they arise. Integrating LVT into Agglomeration theory offers a coherent framework for addressing contemporary urban challenges while reinforcing the productivity benefits of urban concentration. By conceptualising LVT as a dynamic, spatially sensitive policy instrument, this article positions it as an underutilised yet powerful tool for enhancing urban efficiency, equity, and long-run agglomeration potential.

articles.title: Research on spatiotemporal evolution and influencing factors of county-level crime: A case of Guizhou province in southwest China
Age friendly, but for whom? Socio-spatial heterogeneity in functional and symbolic meanings of concessionary fares and priority seating in Hong Kong
articles.abstract: This study examines how older adults in Hong Kong engage with age-friendly transport policies, focusing on concessionary fares and priority seating in a context of rapid population aging and pronounced socio-spatial inequality. While such interventions are widely implemented to reduce mobility barriers, their impacts remain uneven and insufficiently understood across different social and spatial groups. Using survey data from 3,326 older adults collected at a pivotal policy juncture, shortly after the introduction of priority seating and before the implementation of fully subsidized fares, the analysis investigates both behavioral responses to fare incentives and stated preferences for transport improvements. The results reveal systematic socio-spatial differences in both behavioral responses and stated preferences. More affluent older adults and those living in well-connected areas are more likely to adjust their travel to benefit from concessionary fares, while disadvantaged groups face constraints related to accessibility and journey complexity. Preferences for transport improvements also vary by mobility, housing, and household status: older and less mobile individuals prioritize safety, capability, and seating; more mobile or affluent groups emphasize system functionality; public housing residents attach greater importance on affordability and priority seating; and respondents identifying themselves as household heads are less likely to prioritize priority seating. These findings show that transport interventions are not interpreted solely in functional terms but also carry symbolic meanings related to independence, entitlement, and reliance on support. As a result, ostensibly universal policies may reproduce inequalities or fail to meet diverse needs. The study highlights the importance of moving beyond one-size-fits-all approaches and calls for more context-sensitive, differentiated strategies in age-friendly transport planning.

articles.title: Integrating multidimensional fragmentation assessment with precise spatial design to sustain urban mangrove landscapes
Urban climate actions: connecting city characteristics to planning responses
Unraveling the dynamics of urban park visits: Daytime visitation patterns and behavioral determinants derived from mobile phone data
The spatial heterogeneity effects of urban renewal: Evidence from Shenzhen, China
More-than-human governance: beyond top-down and bottom-up logics in disaster risk management
Good(s) planning in cities — A review of urban planning scholarship on large freight generators
articles.abstract: Urban freight transportation is both a traffic concern and a spatial issue. Yet within urban planning, freight remains overlooked. To advance the interface between urban planning and urban freight, it is important to understand how planning scholarship approaches urban developments with significant freight implications. Are these implications accounted for and if so, in what way? To this end, we systematically reviewed ten leading urban planning journals, using as a diagnostic lens the concept of ‘large freight generators’, i.e., facilities that produce and attract a large number of freight trips. Our findings reveal that the spatial and temporal dimensions of freight operations are rarely treated as explicit objects of urban governance. Planning should more explicitly account for the moving, storing, and handling of goods within cities, anticipating rather than merely accommodating freight demand. When freight is overlooked, facilities are displaced to peripheral areas and operations spill excessively into streets and curbs, exacerbating congestion and conflicts, and concentrating environmental externalities. In response, we outline a planner-facing research agenda that calls for systematic consideration of freight operations across space and time and deliberate integration of goods and services, especially in new residential neighborhood developments.

articles.title: Evaluating probe-based data for travel demand analysis: A comparative study with household survey and regional model data in San Antonio
Editorial Board
Changing residential preferences in the digital age: Evidence on teleworking and online shopping from the Netherlands
articles.abstract: Teleworking and online shopping, as two ICT-enabled behaviours, are reshaping everyday routines and raising questions about how digital practices enter long-term housing trade-offs. This matters for urban planning because changing preferences may alter spatial demand and land-use and transport needs. This study investigates how teleworking and online shopping are associated with residential location choices in the Netherlands and how these relationships vary across demographic groups and life stages. A stated choice experiment was designed to capture forward-looking housing decisions under varying levels of teleworking, online shopping, and anticipated life events. Data were collected from 1064 Dutch participants and analysed using tenure-specific discrete choice models: a covariate-dependent Generalized Mixed Logit model for homeowners and a mixed multinomial logit model for renters. The results show that teleworking eases homeowners' penalty for 20 km commutes, but not for 35 km, while analogous patterns among renters are more limited. Online grocery shopping is associated with supermarket-distance preferences, although this relationship should be interpreted cautiously because it may partly reflect income-related and locational differences. Higher online non-grocery shopping remains associated with stronger preferences for very close retail access, especially among homeowners. Anticipated life events, such as expecting a child, also reshape utility. Scale parameters indicate substantial individual variation in choice consistency. Overall, both ICT-enabled behaviours are associated with housing trade-offs, with stronger and more direct evidence for teleworking. These results have implications for housing policy, accessibility planning, and land-use and transport modelling in increasingly digital urban contexts.

articles.title: Anticipating China's profound urban shrinkage with a fine-grid perspective in the latter half of the 21st century
Wartime urban planning geovisualizations: The Russian authoritarian settler-colonial project and Mariupol’s reconstruction under occupation
articles.abstract: This article examines the visual projections of Mariupol’s reconstruction following the 2022 Russian siege and subsequent occupation, focusing on geovisualizations of the city’s future produced by both public and private Russian actors. The analysis builds on research on demolition and reconstruction in wartime, while moving beyond the dichotomy between war-time demolition and peace-time reconstruction. To approach this, the article draws on postcolonial studies, which highlight the erasure logics characteristic of settler colonialism, as well as urban studies that emphasize the key features of authoritarian Russian urban planning. The visual representations of Mariupol’s reconstruction reflect the intersection of these two perspectives, resulting in a form of wartime urban planning that is both colonial and authoritarian. The article is structured around three main sections: the theoretical framework, the methodological approach, followed by a detailed presentation of the context in which the geovisualizations of Mariupol were produced. The fourth section presents one of the main empirical findings: the identification of three dominant visual regimes in these geovisualizations—the comfort gaze, normalization through functionalization and technicization, and pervasive russification. Each of these contributes to the visual and representational dimension of the wartime urban planning implemented by the Russian authorities in Mariupol’s reconstruction.

articles.title: Incremental urbanism: Experimenting with land development and statecraft in Lhasa, Tibet
articles.abstract: The theoretical agendas of comparative urbanism and Southern urban critique encourage scholars to attend to the locatedness of concepts and theories, to stress-test their applicability across various contexts and on this basis to generate new ones or revise existing ones. Methodologically, to unlock the potentiality of theorisation, it is conducive to view urban processes as conjunctural configurations codetermined by diverse forces, as well as interconnections and contextualities across scales. This article presents a case study of Tibet Cultural Tourism and Creative Park in Lhasa, Tibetan Autonomous Region, revealing how the development of the Park follows principles of incrementalism and experimentation, and prioritises small-scale accretion of urban spaces, policy innovations and a complex mixture of economic and non-economic governance goals. As such, this article engages with and enriches the concept of incremental urbanism, which has been developed with reference to numerous Southern contexts. While so far, the concept has been applied mostly to vernacular practices and knowledge of individuals navigating the uncertainty of urban life, this study implies that the experimental, improvised, provisional and emergent aspects of urban changes are also pertinent to theorisations on urban statecraft and governance. Overall, this concept enables us to retheorise municipal statecraft as: (1) flexible, responsive and adaptive; and (2) intertwined with a diversified portfolio of governance objectives beyond growth per se.

articles.title: Mitigation of temperature-induced vegetable price volatility in urban wholesale markets
articles.abstract: Urban vegetable price stability under temperature extremes is poorly understood. Chen et al. show that thermal shocks drive wholesale price volatility, highlighting the need for targeted investments in resilient urban supply chains.

articles.title: Spatio-temporal sensitivity of healthcare accessibility: Insights from a system dynamics model
Uneven resilience: Constructing a climate environmental vulnerability index for South Africa's urban core
articles.abstract: Urban areas in developing countries are increasingly exposed to climate risks, yet vulnerability assessments often remain generalised and fail to capture intra-regional disparities. This study addresses this gap by developing a Climate Environmental Vulnerability Index (CEVI) for municipalities in Gauteng Province, South Africa, over the period 2010–2024. The CEVI integrates 17 standardised indicators across three dimensions: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity, using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to construct sub-indices and a composite vulnerability measure. The results reveal significant spatial and temporal variation in climate vulnerability across municipalities, highlighting the multidimensional and uneven distribution of risk across geographically proximate areas. While some municipalities exhibit persistently high vulnerability due to limited adaptive capacity, others demonstrate relative resilience despite similar levels of climatic exposure. The findings show that differences in adaptive capacity are the primary drivers of variation in vulnerability across municipalities, with improvements in socio-economic conditions playing a more decisive role than exposure alone. These results underscore the importance of spatially differentiated and multidimensional approaches to climate risk assessment. From a policy perspective, the study highlights the need for targeted, municipality-level adaptation strategies rather than uniform provincial interventions. The CEVI framework provides a practical and replicable tool for urban planners and policymakers to support evidence-based resource allocation and enhance climate resilience in rapidly urbanising regions, thereby enabling more targeted and effective urban climate adaptation policies.

articles.title: Toward safer micromobility: Identifying urban e-scooter crash severity factors through automated machine learning and crash narrative analysis
Toward age-friendly housing: Everyday practices of older women in common spaces of collective housing in Santiago, Chile
Tourism pressure and tourism-relevant urban quality for spatial decision support in data-scarce cities: The case of Tunis metropolis
Tourism and the commodification of rural space: A grounded theory study of peri-urban villages
Teleworking and residential sorting in polycentric cities: A model of rent gradients and travel response
Out of business: design constraints and financial burdens in repurposing dead shopping malls
articles.abstract: The paper explores adaptive reuse options for abandoned shopping malls amid the so-called retail apocalypse, defined as the widespread closure of brick-and-mortar retail stores, largely driven by the rise of e-commerce and shifting consumer behavior. The research question deals with returning dead shopping centers to productive use through technically feasible and financially viable conversions. The focus is on repurposing rather than demolishing-and-rebuilding solutions, to reconcile functional obsolescence with substantial residual structural life. The four-stage methodology includes: identification of alternatives and criteria through a literature review; alternative ranking using multi-criteria evaluation, specifically the Analytical Hierarchy Process; concept design and cost appraisal; economic valuation using Discounted Cash Flow analysis and Monte Carlo simulation. The method is tested on a case study identified with a survey of Italian dead and dying malls. Out of nine potential repurposing options, multi-criteria evaluation prioritizes a data center, followed by senior housing and a medical facility. Concept design tests suggest minimal invasive works for a data center, versus extensive reconfiguration for the residential and healthcare options. Base-case cash-flow analysis yields net present values and internal rates of return of €12.8 M/7.7% for the data center, €3.4 M/5.3% for senior housing, and €2.2 M/4.4% for the medical facility. Economic viability ranking is sensitive to changes in the discount rate. Results are also strongly affected by changes in revenue fundamentals. Simulation analysis shows that, depending on those fundamentals, the probability that the net present value exceeds zero is 75%, 85%, and barely 50%, respectively. Property book value hinders the feasibility of repurposing.

articles.title: Intercity mobility networks and urban economic output: A cross-national comparison of commuting versus migration
Intended versus experienced benefits of urban blue-green infrastructure: Lessons from Ōtautahi Christchurch, New Zealand
Influence of multilevel and polycentric governance structures on climate change mitigation and adaptation in 209 German municipalities
articles.abstract: Studies have identified municipalities as key actors in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the impacts of climate change. However, the level of municipal engagement in these policy areas varies widely, and little is known about how different multilevel and polycentric governance structures affect their performance. To address this gap, we examined the mitigation and adaptation commitments, plans and ambitions of 209 German municipalities until the end of 2022 and scored them using an updated and revised assessment framework. We then used one-factor ANOVAs and linear regressions to analyse how their scores relate to a municipality's location in a federal state, its belonging to a county, and its function in Germany's ‘central places’ system. Our results show that belonging to certain federal states can have both positive and negative effects, and belonging to a county is a significant negative factor for local adaptation, while the central places system exerts very little influence. Based on these findings, we suggest that more coordinated multilevel governance structures—as opposed to more fragmented polycentric arrangements—are more likely to trigger local climate action. As such, we call for further and more targeted support for municipalities, and a (more) active role for the federal states in supporting municipal policymaking.
